info.bio:
Carl Lee Perkins (Ridgely, Tennessee 9 de abril de 1932 - 19 de enero de 1998) fue un músico estadounidense pionero del rockabilly, una mezcla de rhythm and blues y música country, que inició su carrera con la Sun Records en Memphis al comienzo de los años 50.
De origen humilde, su padre era un granjero arrendatario, Perkins se crió rodeado por la música gospel cantada por los afroamericanos en los campos del algodón.

A la edad de siete años

scenes.name: Jazz de la costa oeste
scenes.author: Ted Gioia
scenes.desc: A finales de los cuarenta Los Ángeles es una escena bop negra en Central Avenue (Dexter Gordon, Wardell Gray, Teddy Edwards, Sonny Criss, Hampton Hawes), pero en los cincuenta domina el cool de músicos blancos, muchos salidos de Kenton, en el Lighthouse de Hermosa Beach y en sellos como Contemporary, Pacific o Fantasy: música muy escrita, contrapuntística, conjuntos medianos, flautas y fliscornos, tempos relajados. Gerry Mulligan triunfa con un cuarteto sin piano («Bernie's Tune») y lanza a Chet Baker, trompetista y cantante de «My Funny Valentine», de vida desordenada y música ordenada. Art Pepper, de sonido casi infantil con Kenton, pasa por la cárcel, absorbe a Coltrane y Coleman y vuelve en los setenta con una pasión sin filtros. Paul Desmond, «el contralto más lento del mundo», teje citas con ironía. Hacia 1962, entre la cárcel, la emigración y las muertes, la escena se apaga.

scenes.name: Rock'n'roll
scenes.author: Piero Scaruffi
scenes.desc: Fusión de rhythm'n'blues y country, con mucho más peso del primero. Chuck Berry inventa en 1955 el rock'n'roll tal como se conocerá durante cincuenta años (la guitarra como instrumento protagonista, canciones propias que hablan a los adolescentes); Bo Diddley aporta el ritmo «hambone», Little Richard y Esquerita el histerismo y el maquillaje (el primer «decadence-rock»), Jerry Lee Lewis el piano feroz y Sun Records el rockabilly. Elvis Presley es, para Scaruffi, «la primera gran estafa del rock'n'roll». Buddy Holly y Eddie Cochran abren otra vía; en paralelo nacen el soul (Ray Charles), la exótica (Martin Denny, Esquivel), la música electrónica de cinta y, en Gran Bretaña, el skiffle.

podcast.title: Post-1956 Career Shift
podcast.body: After December 4, 1956, Carl Perkins, along with Johnny Cash, increasingly moved towards country music and away from rockabilly. This date is considered a significant border in rock and roll history, marking a period before rock and roll became the dominant genre. "They both moved increasingly towards country music, and away from rockabilly."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.body: Carl Perkins was one of the "living legends long past their prime" inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in 1987, contrasting with Aretha Franklin, who was a current hitmaker. "Carl Perkins"

podcast.title: Appearance of Elvis Presley at Studio
podcast.body: On December 4, 1956, while Carl Perkins and his brothers were recording "Matchbox" at Sun Studios, Elvis Presley walked in unexpectedly. Perkins was astonished to see Elvis, noting his significant physical transformation: dyed dark black hair (from light brown), cleared acne, and a new image as a "major sex symbol." "Earl Perkins was astonished to see Elvis there."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 51: "Matchbox" by Carl Perkins

podcast.title: Audition for Sam Phillips
podcast.body: After Elvis Presley moved to a major label, Carl Perkins, a young country boy, auditioned for Sam Phillips at Sun Records and was seen as having "definite possibilities" as a new rockabilly star. "Luckily, there was a new young country boy who had come to audition for him. Karl Perkins had definite possibilities."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 33: "Mystery Train", by Elvis Presley

podcast.title: Career Derailed by Car Accident
podcast.body: Carl Perkins' career suffered a tragic setback when he was involved in a serious car accident en route to perform on the "Perry Como Show" on television. The collision with a truck resulted in the death of the truck driver and the hospitalization of both Carl and his brother Jay, causing a critical loss of career momentum. "On his way to perform on the Perricomo show on TV, Perkins' car hit a truck."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 36: "Blue Suede Shoes" by Carl Perkins

podcast.title: Career-Derailling Car Crash (Pre-TV Appearance)
podcast.body: Shortly after performing as an opening act for Gene Vincent, Carl Perkins was involved in a car crash while en route to New York for a booked TV appearance. This accident severely disrupted and temporarily halted his burgeoning career. "It was right after this show as he travelled to get to New York for the TV appearance he was booked on, that he got into the car crash that derailed his career."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 41: "Be-Bop-A-Lula" by Gene Vincent and the Bluecaps

podcast.title: Chart Versatility
podcast.body: In 1956, Carl Perkins, similar to Elvis Presley, appeared on the R&B, country, and pop charts, indicating a crossover appeal that was recognized across different musical categories by the industry. "Meanwhile, of course, Elvis Presley and Carl Perkins were appearing on the Arv and B charts, as well as the country and pop ones."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 45: "Blueberry Hill", by Fats Domino

podcast.title: Childhood Poverty and Guitar Origin
podcast.body: Carl Perkins endured extreme poverty during his childhood, growing up in a family of sharecroppers. When he expressed a desire for a guitar, his parents were unable to afford one, leading his father to ingeniously craft his first instrument from a cigar box and a broom handle. "his father made him one from a cigar box in a broom handle."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 36: "Blue Suede Shoes" by Carl Perkins

podcast.title: Close Friendship with Johnny Cash
podcast.body: Despite the professional tensions arising from Sam Phillips' perceived favoritism, Carl Perkins and Johnny Cash became close friends. "That's not to say though that Cash disliked Perkins. Quite the contrary. The two became close friends"

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 37: "I Walk The Line" by Johnny Cash

podcast.title: Confusion Over 7-inch Vinyl Single
podcast.body: After his complimentary copies of "Blue Suede Shoes" arrived damaged, Carl Perkins went to a local shop to purchase a replacement. He was dismayed to find a small, seven-inch plastic record with a large center hole, a stark contrast to the ten-inch shellac records he considered "real." Distraught, he cried, believing his record had been ruined, before eventually understanding that these new vinyl singles were the popular format desired by younger audiences. "He was horrified at what he saw. Instead of a proper record, a big ten-inch thing with a tiny little hole in the middle made out of shell-ac."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 36: "Blue Suede Shoes" by Carl Perkins

podcast.title: Departure from Sun Records
podcast.body: Carl Perkins, simultaneously with Johnny Cash, left Sun Records at the approximate time Roy Orbison was looking to end his contract. All three artists believed Sam Phillips was unfair regarding royalties, withheld crucial business information, and prioritized new talent over their established careers. "This was at almost exactly the same time that both Johnny Cash and Carl Perkins left Sun records, and he suspected a degree of collusion between the three men, and he wasn't wrong in his suspicion."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 42: "Ooby Dooby" by Roy Orbison and the Teen Kings

podcast.title: Departure from Sun Records
podcast.body: Karl Perkins became increasingly frustrated with Sam Phillips' favoritism towards Jerry Lee Lewis, feeling his own career was being neglected. He was particularly irked by the credit "Jerry Lee Lewis and his pumping piano" while his own records never mentioned "Karl's guitar." Despite Phillips' belated promise to credit him as "the Rocking guitar man," it was too late. Perkins, along with Johnny Cash, made an agreement with Columbia Records on November 1, 1957, to join the new label once their Sun contracts expired. "Patrons and Johnny Cash, both made an agreement with Columbia Records, on November 1, 1957, that when their current contracts with Sun expired, they'd start recording for the new label."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 66: "Great Balls of Fire" by Jerry Lee Lewis

podcast.title: Description of Elvis Presley's Introversion
podcast.body: Carl Perkins famously described Elvis Presley as "the most introverted person ever to enter a recording studio." "Carl Perkins would later describe him as the most introverted person ever to enter a recording studio."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 33: "Mystery Train", by Elvis Presley

podcast.title: Dissatisfaction with Sam Phillips
podcast.body: Carl Perkins became increasingly dissatisfied with Sam Phillips' promotion of his work. This led him to strongly consider moving to another record label, a sentiment shared by Johnny Cash at the time. "Perkins was increasingly dissatisfied with the way Sam Phillips was promoting his work, and like Johnny Cash was strongly considering moving to another label."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 51: "Matchbox" by Carl Perkins

podcast.title: Early Musical Influences
podcast.body: Carl Perkins was a fervent admirer of Bill Monroe, acknowledged as the originator of Bluegrass music, appreciating his high, driving, and harmony-rich songs of longing. This preference contrasted with his brother Jay's taste for Ernest Tubb's more subdued honky-tonk sound. "Carl was a massive fan of the inventor of Bluegrass, Bill Mundo, who sang high, driving, harmony-filled songs of longing."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 36: "Blue Suede Shoes" by Carl Perkins

podcast.title: Evaluation of Gene Vincent's Talent
podcast.body: Tex Davis asked Carl Perkins to assess Gene Vincent's performance as an opening act. Perkins recognized Vincent's potential, particularly noting the song "Be-Bop-A-Lula," which he felt sounded quite similar to his own musical style. "Karl watched, and he said that the boy had potential, especially one particular song, Be Bappelula, which sounded to Karl quite like some of his own stuff."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 41: "Be-Bop-A-Lula" by Gene Vincent and the Bluecaps

podcast.title: Improvised Songwriting Style
podcast.body: Most of Carl Perkins' records, including "Matchbox," were at least semi-improvised or "largely improvised" during studio sessions. This approach was common for him, often just making up material to fill vinyl space. "Matchbox shows all the sounds of having been put together in the studio, largely impovervised, as most of Perkins' songs were."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 51: "Matchbox" by Carl Perkins

podcast.title: Million Dollar Quartet Participant
podcast.body: Carl Perkins was present during the famous Million Dollar Quartet sessions when Elvis Presley continually raved about Jackie Wilson, then a singer with Billy Ward and the Dominoes. "In the famous million dollar quartet tapes, you can hear Elvis raving about Wilson to Johnny Cash, Karl Perkins, and Jerry Lee Lewis."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode Sixty-Four: "Reet Petite" by Jackie Wilson

podcast.title: Overton Park Shell Concert (June 1)
podcast.body: Kyle Perkins, billed as "Mr. Blue Swade Shoes" and fresh from the Pericomo TV show, headlined a country rock and roll show at the Overton Park Shell in Memphis on Friday, June 1, at 8 p.m. He performed alongside other notable artists like Johnny Cash, Warren Smith, Roy Orbison, and Eddie Bond and the Stumpers. "Kyle Perkins will rock and roll in the Overton Park show for a great show Friday night, the first to June 8 p.m."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Weird History of Concert Tickets Part 2

podcast.title: Post-Sun Career
podcast.body: Unlike Johnny Cash, Karl Perkins did not achieve greater success after leaving Sun Records for Columbia. "While Cash would go on to have greater success at Columbia, Perkins wouldn't, and ironically it was possible that he had had one more opportunity to have a hit follow-up to Blue Swade Shoes at Sun, and he passed on it."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 66: "Great Balls of Fire" by Jerry Lee Lewis

podcast.title: Pre-Fame Financial Struggles
podcast.body: Despite having released records and performing on stage, Carl Perkins earned so little from his music that he was compelled to work a side job on a farm to generate enough income to buy Christmas presents for his children. This situation often astonished those around him, who recognized him from his performances and records and assumed he was financially successful. "He was earning so little money from his music that he was having to do farm work as a side job in order to make enough money to buy his kids Christmas presents."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 36: "Blue Suede Shoes" by Carl Perkins

podcast.title: Preferred by Janice Martin over Elvis Presley
podcast.body: Janice Martin, despite being compared to Elvis Presley in her performance style, explicitly stated that she preferred Carl Perkins, indicating her own musical tastes and influences. "She preferred Karl Perkins."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 40: "Drugstore Rock 'n' Roll" by Janis Martin

podcast.title: Resentment Towards Jerry Lee Lewis
podcast.body: Carl Perkins became friends with Jerry Lee Lewis during a tour with Johnny Cash and Wanda Jackson, but he also started to resent Lewis's status as Sam Phillips's "new golden boy" and plotted ways to leave their contract with Sun Records to avoid being overshadowed. "Perkins and Cash were already starting to resent the fact that Jerry Lee was clearly Sam Phillips's new golden boy and plotting ways to get out of their contract with Son and go somewhere that they'd not be overshadowed by this wild kid."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 59: "Whole Lotta Shakin' Goin' On" by Jerry Lee Lewis

podcast.title: Rivalry with Elvis Presley
podcast.body: Carl Perkins and Elvis Presley maintained a friendship despite an incident on tour where Perkins "upstaged" Presley by performing "Only You," a song Elvis had also planned to perform that night. This event led to the two artists never sharing a stage again. However, Elvis did offer fashion advice, taking Carl shopping to help him develop a more sophisticated stage appearance. "The two remained friends, but would never perform on the same bill again."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 36: "Blue Suede Shoes" by Carl Perkins

podcast.title: Rivalry with Jerry Lee Lewis on "Matchbox"
podcast.body: During the recording of "Matchbox," Carl Perkins was hugely impressed by Jerry Lee Lewis's musical talent but initially unimpressed by his personality, especially after Lewis critiqued Perkins' "Your True Love." Perkins felt Lewis lacked originality and was showing off. To assert himself, Perkins decided to elevate his guitar playing, adopting a "hard-driving riff" and playing "Triple String" solos on the top three strings of his guitar, explicitly stating he was "shooting at Jerry Lee's head" and taking two solos to prevent Lewis from getting a piano break. "But fooling around and practising, I knew it would work, and that was the time to try it, because I was shooting at Jerry Lee's head."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 51: "Matchbox" by Carl Perkins

podcast.title: Rockabilly Fizzle
podcast.body: Carl Perkins was part of the wave of white rockabilly acts that achieved popularity between 1955 and 1956 but had largely "fizzled" on the US charts by late 1956, failing to secure another major domestic hit. Despite this, he went on to find success in other countries and produced important music in subsequent years. "While Perkins, Gene Vincent and Bill Haley would between them never have another major hit in the US, though all of them would have success in other countries and make important music over the next few years."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 45: "Blueberry Hill", by Fats Domino

podcast.title: Royalty Disputes with Sam Phillips
podcast.body: Sam Phillips presented Carl Perkins with a Cadillac, claiming it was a reward for "Blue Suede Shoes" becoming the first Sun Records million-seller. However, Perkins later discovered the car's cost was deducted from his own royalties. This incident initiated a lifelong series of royalty disputes between the two men, with Perkins consistently believing he was denied his rightful earnings. "Perkins was less impressed when he found out that the Cadillac wasn't a gift, but had been paid for out of Perkins' royalties, and that eventually started a lifelong series of royalty disputes between the two men."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 36: "Blue Suede Shoes" by Carl Perkins

podcast.title: Sam Phillips' Audition Condition
podcast.body: After being rejected on his first two attempts, Carl Perkins played "Movie Mag" for Sam Phillips, who listened with keen interest. Phillips then offered the band a chance to record if they returned with more songs in that vein, but he specifically told Carl that his brother Jay's lead vocals were not suitable, making it clear that the group would effectively become "Carl Perkins and his band." "He told Carl that there was no place for any lead vocals by his brother Jay."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 36: "Blue Suede Shoes" by Carl Perkins

podcast.title: Signing to Sun Records
podcast.body: Carl Perkins was signed to Sun Records around the same time Johnny Cash was building his following. Perkins' signing caused problems for Cash, who felt Phillips was treating him as less important and focusing more on his new star. "It's around this time that son signed Karl Perkins which caused problems."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 37: "I Walk The Line" by Johnny Cash

podcast.title: Single-Song Defining Career
podcast.body: Following the immense success of "Blue Suede Shoes," Carl Perkins never achieved another hit as a performer, and his career largely became defined by that one song. Despite this, he continued to create records that would later inspire globally significant musicians and become classics. "Perkins would never have another hit as a performer, and his career would be defined by that one song."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 36: "Blue Suede Shoes" by Carl Perkins

podcast.title: Successful Crossover Artist
podcast.body: Carl Perkins is mentioned as a rockabilly artist whose music successfully crossed over from the country market, unlike Wanda Jackson's "I Gotta Know" which primarily sold to the country market.

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 43: "I Gotta Know" by Wanda Jackson

podcast.title: Sun Records Audition Initial Rejection
podcast.body: Upon arriving at Sun Records for an audition, Carl Perkins and his band were initially dismissed by Marion Keisker, an employee, who stated the label wasn't holding auditions and had no need for new singers, especially not another act resembling Elvis Presley. Their opportunity for a quick listen only arose from a fortuitous encounter with Sam Phillips as they were leaving. "Marion Kaiske told them that they weren't auditioning right then, and that they didn't need any new singers."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 36: "Blue Suede Shoes" by Carl Perkins

podcast.title: Sun Records Success after Elvis
podcast.body: Carl Perkins generated "massive hits" for Sun Records after Elvis Presley's departure, a success largely attributed to the financial influx the label received from the Elvis-RCA deal. "It was able to generate massive hits for Karl Perkins and Johnny Cash after Elvis left, but that's only because of the cash the label was able to make from the Elvis deal."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 38: "Heartbreak Hotel" by Elvis Presley

podcast.title: Turning Down "Great Balls of Fire"
podcast.body: Karl Perkins claimed he was offered "Great Balls of Fire" to perform in the film "Jamboree" but turned it down, believing it was "dreck" along with another song provided by Hill & Range. Other people involved in the situation remember it differently. "He would always claim that he had been offered the song that Jerry Lee Lewis performed, and turned down Great Balls of Fire."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 66: "Great Balls of Fire" by Jerry Lee Lewis

podcast.title: Unique Guitar Style Development
podcast.body: Due to his family's destitution, Carl Perkins could not afford new guitar strings when they broke and resorted to tying them back together. To avoid the pain caused by the knots, he innovated a distinctive guitar playing style involving bending strings to achieve different notes, rather than employing conventional fretting techniques. "he ended up developing a unique guitar style, bending strings to get different notes rather than fretting them normally, to avoid the knots in the strings which hurt his fingers."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
